analysis.one_liner: Lets corporations deduct dividends they pay, largely erasing the corporate tax on distributed profits.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed the tax code so that any dividend a domestic corporation pays to its shareholders could be deducted from the company's taxable income, just like a business expense. That would largely eliminate the corporate income tax on profits paid out as dividends, ending what is often called the "double taxation" of corporate earnings (the same profit taxed once at the company and again at the shareholder). It would also scrap some existing tax breaks for dividends corporations receive, and raise the deduction for dividends American corporations get from foreign companies they partly own. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations that pay dividends and their shareholders. Because deductible dividends would escape corporate tax, companies would have a strong incentive to pay out profits, and the tax savings would flow to shareholders. Dividend income is concentrated among wealthier households, so the benefit would be concentrated there too. Companies receiving dividends from foreign subsidiaries they own would also gain a bigger deduction.

how_it_helps.text: Allows a domestic corporation to deduct from its taxable income an amount equal to all dividends it pays during the year, so profits distributed to shareholders would no longer be taxed at the corporate level.
Excludes pass-through and investment vehicles — S corporations, regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, and personal holding companies — from the new deduction.
Raises the deductible share of dividends a corporation receives from a foreign company it at least 10 percent owns from 80 percent to 85 percent.
Partially offsets the cost by repealing existing deductions for dividends corporations receive from domestic companies and special preferred-stock rules for public utilities.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Every dividend deducted is revenue the government does not collect, and the bill contains no replacement funding, so the cost would fall on other taxpayers or on federal borrowing.

drawbacks.text: The bill would cut federal revenue by an amount equal to the corporate tax now collected on all distributed profits, with no offsetting revenue in the bill text.

The gains would go overwhelmingly to shareholders of dividend-paying companies, and dividend income is concentrated among higher-income households, so the tax savings would be concentrated among the wealthiest rather than spread broadly.

The partial offset — repealing the dividends-received deduction for corporations — raises taxes on companies that hold stock in other companies, a cost the bill acknowledges through its own conforming amendments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would genuinely end the double taxation of distributed corporate profits, which economists have long criticized as discouraging investment. But the benefit is a large, untargeted tax cut whose value flows mainly to wealthier shareholders, and it would be paid for by every other federal taxpayer through lost revenue. The bill offered no broader benefit to working people to weigh against that cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never considered it, so it died when the Congress ended in early 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Dornan introduced the bill on January 27, 1993, as his first action on it, with no other member signing on as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it, and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers kept the corporate tax revenue on distributed profits that the bill would have eliminated; shareholders of dividend-paying corporations gained nothing. A tax cut aimed at dividend recipients never advanced far enough to threaten that revenue.

for.name: Rep. Robert K. Dornan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; never held a hearing or a vote, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no meaningful partisan pattern ever formed around it.

industries.note: Deducting dividends would wipe out most corporate tax on distributed profits, with the savings flowing to shareholders — a group concentrated among wealthier households — while the lost revenue falls on everyone else.
The bill raises the deduction for dividends received from 10-percent-owned foreign corporations from 80 to 85 percent, shrinking their U.S. tax bill.

The bill repeals the special deductions tied to preferred stock issued by public utilities, raising taxes on some utility dividend arrangements while the new paid-dividend deduction would benefit utilities that pay common dividends.

industries.industry: Corporations holding stock in other companies
industries.note: Repealing the dividends-received deduction raises taxes on corporate shareholders of other companies, partially offsetting the bill's cost.
